title: One more year (Luke 13:1–9)
hookLine: a barren fig tree gets one more year of digging and manure

cards: The news comes first. Some people tell Jesus that Pilate, the Roman governor, has killed Galileans while they were offering sacrifices.

Jesus adds another disaster: a tower at Siloam, in Jerusalem, collapsed and killed eighteen people. When disaster strikes, someone says it out loud, or thinks it quietly: they must have done something.
Jesus asks it directly. Were they worse than everyone else? "I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish."
Then, instead of explaining suffering, he tells a story about a tree.

teach.b: A man has a fig tree planted in his vineyard. Three years running he comes looking for fruit and finds none.
So he tells the gardener, in the King James Bible: "cut it down; why cumbereth it the ground?" It's a fair question. The tree has taken up ground for three years and given nothing back.

teach.h: LET IT ALONE: DIG AND DUNG.
teach.b: But the gardener answers: "Lord, let it alone this year also, till I shall dig about it, and dung it." Dung it. Manure.

He doesn't just ask for more time; he offers to get his hands dirty, loosening the hard ground round the roots and feeding it with the least glamorous stuff on the farm. A small thing in the Greek is worth knowing.

Let it alone is a form of aphiēmi, the ordinary verb for let go, leave be. It's also the word the Gospels use for forgive, as in forgive us our sins. So to a Greek ear the request sounds a little like a plea for mercy.

Some Christian readers hear Jesus himself in the gardener, pleading for time and doing the digging. Then the story stops: if it bears fruit, well; if not, cut it down after that. We never find out what happened next year.
Luke leaves the ending open, the way a life is open. It's a story about urgency, the year is real and it ends, and about patience, the kind that works the soil instead of just waiting.

teach.h: LET IT ALONE THIS YEAR ALSO.
teach.b: Disaster doesn't prove anyone deserved it; and the year the gardener asks for is a year of digging.

how: In the Catholic Sunday readings, Luke 13:1–9 falls in Lent, the season of repentance, and some Christians hear the gardener as Christ pleading for time.

games.why: "Lord, let it alone this year also, till I shall dig about it, and dung it." and the story never says what happened next.

practice: Think of someone you've been close to writing off, a colleague who never delivers, a relative who keeps letting you down, or maybe yourself, and picture them as the fig tree and yourself as the gardener asking for one more season.
What would digging around the roots look like: a real conversation, some help, a little patience with a deadline? If you pray, ask for the gardener's patience.

wordCard.voice: Aphiēmi, the Greek verb for let it alone, leave be — the gardener's plea for a fruitless fig tree he offers to dig and feed, while the story never tells us how it turned out.

orig.note: Greek: let it alone, leave it. a form of aphiēmi, the same verb the Gospels use for forgive.

carryVoice: Your line: leave it one more year. Patience, in this story, gets its hands dirty. See you tomorrow.
